prize_parts.citation: For the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, in which atoms held in a magic-wavelength lattice enable frequency measurement at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I have moved my preferred configuration from the topological-insulator prize (B061) to the optical lattice clock (B040) by Katori and Ye as a stand-alone prize. My reasons are scientific and about credit, not about counting support. The test I apply in my own field is whether a result is robust, independently reproduced, and understood quantitatively. The lattice clock passes it as clearly as anything on the slate: JILA, RIKEN and Tokyo, SYRTE, PTB, NIST and NPL compare clocks at the 10^-18 level, including over fibre links, so the claim does not rest on one group. The discovery-versus-instrument objection, which I raised myself in round 1, is answered by what the clocks have produced: many-body quantum states in a degenerate Fermi gas that set the systematic limits, a millimetre-scale measurement of the gravitational redshift, limits on drifting constants and searches for ultralight dark matter. These are new physical measurements that were not possible before. In one sentence for the chair: the magic-wavelength lattice made it possible to interrogate vast numbers of neutral atoms without a trap shift, which opened a regime of many-body precision control that neither the frequency comb (2005) nor single-ion control (2012) provided. The credit is compact: Katori conceived the scheme and built the first strontium lattice clock, and Ye took it to record accuracy and coherence. The physics is mature, the prize would be a stand-alone achievement with two names, and no member has voiced a scientific objection to it.
statement.case_against: The overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes is real, and some will read the clock as the next increment in optical metrology. The redefinition of the second has not yet been adopted, so the practical payoff is still prospective, though I treat that as procedural. Two names leave out Ludlow, Hinkley, Bloom, Lemonde, Gill and Takamoto, and I cannot adjudicate the early Tokyo versus JILA priority; that must come from the external expert reports. I also give up a topological-insulator prize that I still consider conceptually the larger shift in how we classify electronic matter and that I regard as overdue. Condensed matter would then be unrepresented this year, which is a reason to keep B061 as my first alternative and not a reason to prefer it. A final caution is that the committee's convergence on B040 is partly the product of members changing position after reading each other, so it deserves testing, which is what the clock's overlap questions are for.

responses.point: Mehlig argues that the BHZ proposal told Molenkamp's group which quantum wells to grow, that Kane-Mele alone did not fix the platform because the graphene gap is tiny, and that B040 is the better-attributed fallback if the credit cannot be drawn cleanly.
responses.response: He is right on the physics of the chain, and his point changes my position. In round 1 I said a citation naming the prediction and the observation could absorb the BHZ omission. Having thought about his argument, I do not think that wording repairs it: the citation would be accurate, but a prize that rewards the experiment without the proposal that selected HgTe would still read as an incomplete allocation within a three-name limit, and I cannot add Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang without breaking that limit. I stay with him on the scientific weight of B061 and on the 2016 prize not amounting to duplication, and I hope he will keep it as the leading alternative. But since he himself names B040 as the fallback, I think we should treat the credit problem as unresolved and move to the candidate whose credit is clean.

responses.point: Kroll argues that conceptual novelty should not dominate, that B061 has an attribution problem B040 does not, and that the lattice clock is a reproducible, intercompared result with the redshift, constants and dark-matter measurements it has enabled.
responses.response: I conceded in round 1 that I valued conceptual surprise most, and I still think a conceptual discovery deserves a place on the same footing. But his point about attribution carries the argument, and his emphasis on reproducible intercomparison is the criterion I use myself for electronic-structure results, so I cannot say B040 fails it. I would ask him for the draft wording the chair requested, stating the many-body and redshift results explicitly so that the citation answers the discovery-versus-instrument question, and not just 'enabling measurement at 10^-18'. I also note his own concern that B017 needs four names; I agree it cannot be a second part here.

responses.point: Lindroth, answering my round-1 reply, said she would treat B061 as a serious second configuration if the HgTe credit were settled, and asked whether BHZ can be handled within three names. She also asked for a colleague outside AMO to test whether the clock reads as fundamental physics or as an instrument.
responses.response: I take her request to be addressed to me and I can answer it: I do not think BHZ can be handled within three names, so on her own condition B061 does not qualify as a clean configuration this year. As the outside colleague she asked for, I have tested the clock on the points I care about: reproduction across independent laboratories, and agreement between measurements and a quantitative model of the systematics. It holds up on both, and the redshift and constants results make it physics and not only an instrument. My remaining concern is priority between Tokyo and JILA, which I leave to her and the expert reports.

responses.point: Danielsson, who prefers B040 plus B028, ranked B061 sixth because the HgTe proposal sits outside the slate, accepts it is Nobel-worthy, and asked how I would handle BHZ. He also lists the arbitrary pairing and the unexplained pairing mechanism as reservations on his own B040 plus B028 configuration.
responses.response: He asked how I would handle BHZ, and my answer is now that I would not, within three names, which is why I am moving. On his two-part configuration I would hold B028 as an alternative. Hosono's discovery is a clean experimental result that was confirmed within weeks, and the missing mechanism does not bother me as a condensed-matter theorist, since discovery came first for the cuprates too. But the committee would be pairing it with the clock without a common thread, which he himself calls a compromise, and the early Tc gains by other groups complicate the single-name credit. I prefer to let the clock stand alone and keep B028 available if the committee wants a second part.

responses.point: Olsson says the BHZ omission is a serious attribution issue for B061 and ranks it sixth in round 1, then pairs B040 with Hosono's B028 on the argument that both are experimentally verified, mature and cleanly credited.
responses.response: Her BHZ objection was the one I called my strongest reservation in round 1, and it has now outweighed my reply to it. I do not follow her to the pairing, because the discovery in B028 is genuine but the pairing mechanism remains unexplained, other groups made the early Tc gains, and the two parts share no thread. She is right that three people in total keeps the prize within bounds, and I would not object if the committee chose it, but I think the stand-alone clock is the more defensible public position.

responses.point: Pearce, the chair, notes that I ranked the clock eighth at opening, asks the condensed-matter members to weigh the 2016 overlap, and says he cannot judge Kane-Mele against BHZ himself and will not stand in the way if the condensed-matter members agree on the trio.
responses.response: He asked whether the low ranking reflects a scientific objection or only distance from the field. It was distance, as I said in round 1, and I have found no scientific flaw. On the condensed-matter judgment he asked for: I and Mehlig hold B061 to be conceptually decisive, but we do not agree on the trio being clean, so he need not defer to us on it. I do not regard the 2016 overlap as decisive, since Z2 time-reversal-invariant topology is a different class from Chern topology. I would instead rely on the credit gap to decide this year.

uncertainties: Whether Katori and Ye are sufficient against Ludlow, Hinkley, Bloom, Lemonde, Gill and Takamoto; I cannot resolve Tokyo versus JILA priority and rely on the external expert reports.
How heavily to weigh the 2005 and 2012 precedents and the not yet adopted redefinition of the second.
Whether the convergence on B040 reflects independent judgment or mutual adjustment after the opening ballots.
Whether the BHZ credit gap in B061 could be closed by a configuration I have not seen; I would revisit it if shown one that stays within three names.
statement.conflict_note: No personal or institutional conflict with Katori, Ye, Kane, Mele, Molenkamp or Hosono is apparent from my profile. I am a theorist in electronic structure and magnetism and have no recorded tie to the lattice-clock groups. I chaired the 2025 committee that awarded the circuit tunnelling prize; this is relevant to B055 as a matter of timing, not a personal conflict, and B055 is not in my configuration. My distance from atomic physics is a limit on my judgment of priority, not a conflict.
